item.title: Quadratic reset bounds for finite maximal prefix codes
item.description: arXiv:2611.05675v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let $C$ be a finite maximal prefix code of maximum codeword length $k\ge2$. We prove that, whenever the literal decoder of $C$ is synchronizing, it has a reset word of length at most $(k-1)(4k-5)$. The bound is independent of the alphabet and the number of decoder states. Its main ingredient is a short-detection theorem: a linear observation of the decoder, with terminal weight constant on states of depth $k-1$, is either identically zero or nonzero on a word of length at most $2k-3$. The proof uses a first-return decomposition in noncommuting variables and cancellation of a highest-degree coefficient. For codes whose codeword lengths are $k-1$ and $k$, we prove the sharper bound $2(k-1)^2-1$ and characterize equality. The binary code with the single short word $a^{k-1}$ attains this bound for every $k\ge2$; an age representation and a potential on circular arcs give the matching lower bound. Both upper bounds yield polynomial-time constructions in the explicit code size. The mathematical results and the algorithms are formalized in Lean, with polynomial work bounds in a specified binary cost model.
item.dc:creator: Samrath Singh Chadha

item.title: An Engineering Reading of the Bounded Halting Problem and Observable Properties of a Universal Machine
item.description: arXiv:2611.06303v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The halting problem asks whether a program eventually halts, with unrestricted resources. Engineering systems instead certify bounded halting: given a program, an input, and a step budget T, decide whether the program halts within T steps. This paper studies two of its uses. First, it defines an exact finite-budget problem, placing the simulated program and the checker on the same unit-cost timescale, so the checker can be embedded in an adversarial program. A diagonal argument with explicit additive overhead shows that no fixed deterministic checker decides every instance within any fixed fraction of T below one, for large T. In the nondeterministic case, T bounds the branch depth allowed for a stable observable decision. Second, bounded-halting instances give adversarial tests for finitary universality, since a universal model must support arbitrary finite computations as T grows. The tests check resource growth with T, the absence of a fixed deliberation bound, and later access to intermediate data. They separate a fixed model with extendable external resources, a model family that grows with T, and a larger system built around a fixed component. For machine-learning systems, this identifies the resource growth a universality claim assumes and whether it fails for deployed models.

item.title: Explorable Parity Automata
item.description: arXiv:2410.23187v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We define the class of explorable automata on finite or infinite words. This is a generalization of History-Deterministic (HD) automata, where this time non-deterministic choices can be resolved by building finitely many simultaneous runs instead of just one. We show that recognizing HD parity automata of fixed index among explorable ones is in PTime, thereby giving a strong link between the two notions. We then show that recognizing explorable automata is ExpTime-complete, in the case of finite words or parity automata up to index [0, 2]. Additionally, we define the notion of Ï‰-explorable automata on infinite words, where countably many runs can be used to resolve the non-deterministic choices. We show ExpTime-completeness for Ï‰-explorability of automata on infinite words for the safety and coBÃ¼chi acceptance conditions. We finally characterize the expressivity of (Ï‰-)explorable automata with respect to the parity index hierarchy.

item.title: The Scope Grammar of Natural-Language Rules: Counting and Enumerating Readings modulo Logical Equivalence
item.description: arXiv:2611.01825v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A rule written for people fixes its atomic conditions and connectives but leaves open how the connectives are bracketed, and each bracketing is a different logical reading that an autoformalizer must resolve or expose. We study the scope grammar, a deliberately ambiguous context-free grammar whose derivation trees are the readings of a connective skeleton and whose quotient by logical equivalence is what matters downstream. A skeleton with $k$ binary connectives has $C_k$ derivation trees, the $k$-th Catalan number, but far fewer logically distinct readings. For the positive, repetition-free fragment we make the gap exact: through the uniqueness of the read-once normal form we characterize the realizable normal forms by lowest common ancestors and count them with a two-label recurrence over the operator word, verified against exhaustive enumeration up to eleven atoms. The count is invariant under reversal and $\wedge/\vee$ duality; a skeleton is ambiguous if and only if it uses both $\wedge$ and $\vee$, a one-pass test; and the number of classes is at least $2^{\lfloor n/3\rfloor}$. Up to fifteen atoms the alternating pattern is the worst case; its count has a cubic generating function, is the 3-Schr\"oder sequence (OEIS A137842), and grows with base $\varphi^{5/2}\approx3.330$, below the Catalan base 4. We reduce maximality to an inequality on increments, verified to sixteen atoms, and explain why local exchange arguments cannot prove it. We also treat negation, exceptions, and background axioms, where normal-form uniqueness still decides equivalence but counting is open.
item.dc:creator: Sherzod Turaev
